Aer a tion promotes Proteobacteria over Firmicutes in 
macer a ted food waste, resulting in superior anaerobic 
digestion efficiency 
Linjie Tang 
* and Mike Manefield 
School of Civil and Environmental Engineering, UNSW Sydne y, Sydne y, NSW 2052, Australia 
∗Corr esponding author. Sc hool of Civil and Envir onmental Engineering, UNSW Sydney, Sydney, NSW 2052, Australia. E-mail: linjie .tang@uns w.edu.au 
Editor: [Ser a phim P a panik olaou] 
Abstract 
Aeration is a common pr etr eatment method to enhance biogas production via anaerobic digestion of waste organic feedstocks such 
as unused food. While impacts on downstream anaerobic digestion have been intensively investigated, the consequence of aeration 
on the microbial community in food waste has not been c har acterized. Food waste has a low pH resulting from the dominance of lactic 
acid bacteria within the Firmicutes phylum. This excludes other phylotypes with a higher potential to hydr ol yse complex biopolymers 
in food waste. In this study, we r ev eal that aeration of macerated food waste results in a dramatic shift a wa y from Firmicutes to war ds 
dominance of Proteobacteria that are better known for extracellular enzyme pr oduction. Gi v en that hydr ol ysis is the rate limiting step 
in anaerobic digestion, this explains why aeration impr ov es the efficiency of biogas production from food waste. The discovery that 
Proteobacteria dominate microbial communities in aerated food waste opens up opportunities to manipulate extracellular enzyme 
pr oduction thr ough gene expr ession mechanisms common among Pr oteobacteria such as quorum sensing. 
Ke yw ords: food waste; anaerobic digestion; pretreatment; microbial ecology 
Introduction 
Pr etr eating food waste via physical, chemical, or biological meth- 
ods enhances the efficiency of subsequent anaerobic diges- 
tion carried out by micr oor ganisms (Suhartini et al. 2022 ). De- 
spite efforts to de v elop pr etr eatment methods, little attention 
has been given to the microbiology of food waste prior to or 
during pr etr eatment, whic h logicall y influences the effective- 
ness of pr etr eatments that exploit micr oflor a indigenous to food 
waste. 
Lactic acid bacteria belonging to the Firmicutes phylum are 
numerically dominant in food waste (Fisgativa et al. 2018 , Wu 
et al. 2018 , Tang et al. 2023 ). Their metabolism, which generates 
volatile fatty acids, underpins the low pH of food waste, nega- 
tiv el y influencing the efficiency of anaerobic digestion (Zhou et 
al. 2018 ). Inter estingl y, food waste harbours few re presentati ves 
of one of the most diverse and abundant groups of micr obes, Pr o- 
teobacteria (Zhou et al. 2020a ). Fr esh v egetable and meat products 
are known to harbour Proteobacteria, such as Serratia , Hafnia , and 
Pseudomonas (Jackson et al. 2013 , Remenant et al. 2015 , Odeyemi et 
al. 2020 ), which play roles in food-borne disease and food spoilage 
(Jarvis et al. 2018 ). Pr oteobacteria ar e also commonl y observ ed in 
food waste anaerobic digesters (Wu et al. 2016 , Campanaro et al. 
2020 , Yadav et al. 2022 ). 
Extr acellular enzymes ar e r esponsible for biopol ymer hy- 
dr ol ysis in anaerobic digestion (Menzel et al. 2020 ). The pro- 
duction of extr acellular degr adativ e enzymes by Proteobacteria 
has been intensiv el y studied. Thr ough micr obiological and ge- 
nomic studies, Gamma pr oteobacteria hav e been shown to pos- 
sess the genetic ability to produce and secrete various extracel- 
lular hydr ol ytic enzymes (Mahmoudi et al. 2020 ). Ho w e v er, lac- 
tic acid bacteria have limited extracellular production, which 
is limited to the hydr ol ysis of pol ysacc harides and pr oteins 
(Wang et al. 2021 ). 
In food waste environments characterized by high water ac- 
ti vity, high n utrient availability, and low o xygen content, volatile 
fatty acid production by lactic acid bacteria lo w ers the pH. This 
results in the loss of Proteobacteria (Tang et al. 2023 ). The in- 
troduction of oxygen to maize and activated sludge prior to 
anaerobic digestion has been shown to increase the abundance 
of Proteobacteria (Ruan et al. 2019 , Zhu et al. 2022 ). This phe- 
nomenon has not been investigated in the context of food waste 
pr etr eatment. 
In this study, food waste samples were subjected to 3-day incu- 
bations with aeration and pH adjustment to neutral conditions, 
and the impacts on the volatile fatty acid concentr ation, extr a- 
cellular enzyme pr oduction, micr obial comm unity composition, 
and subsequent anaerobic digestion were quantified. Through the 
understanding of the changes in volatile fatty acid and extra- 
cellular enzyme profile after pretreatment, the variations in this 
microbial-de pendent acti vity can be link ed to the alternation of 
pr etr eated food waste digestibility. Furthermore, the comparison 
between microbial communities in untreated and pretreated food 
waste could further indicate impactful microbes that emerged or 
dissipated during the post–pr etr eatment pr ocess. Pr etr eated food 
waste exhibited increased digestibility as observed in shortened 
anaerobic digestion time, along with altered VF A (V olatile fatty 
acid) pr ofile, incr eased digestiv e enzyme activities, and gr owth of 
corr esponding micr obes.

Materials and methods 
Food waste pretreatment 
Food waste was obtained from a UNSW cafeteria, Sydney, Aus- 
tralia. The identifiable components in the food w aste w er e br ead, 
deli meat, leafy greens , tortillas , and tomatoes . Unwanted compo- 
nents such as napkins were manually discarded, and a food chop- 
per was used to macerate the food waste into mince. Milli-Q water 
was added to food waste to make a 5% solid content food waste 
slurry. The food waste slurry (25 ml) was subjected to three types 
of pr etr eatments: pH adjustment ( ∼pH 7); aer ation, and aer ation 
plus pH adjustment for 3 days at 32 ◦C; and storing an untreated 
group and opening it to air at the same temper atur e . T he pH was 
adjusted by adding phosphate buffer until the pH r eac hed 7. The 
pH of the buffer was maintained above 6.5 for 3 da ys . Aeration was 
performed by shaking the samples, which were placed in 250 ml 
Erlenmeyer flasks and shaken at 160 rpm. Samples were taken 
on day 0 and day 3 and then stored at -20 ◦C before analysis . T he 
choice of a 3-day treatment period was based on both industry ca- 
pability and the objective of minimizing VFA production (Charles 
et al. 2009 ). 
Vola tile fa tty acid quantifica tion 
Acetate , formate , butyrate , and propionate were analysed 
with GC-FID (gas c hr omotogr a phy with downstream flame 
ionisation detector) (Carlström et al. 1965 ) using a DB-FFAP 
(nitr oter ephthalic-acid-modified pol yethylene gl ycol) column 
(30 m × 0.32 mm × 0.25 mm, Ag ilent Technolog ies). An au- 
tosampler (Shimadzu AOC-5000 Plus) was used to dir ectl y 
inject headspace samples into the GC-FID instrument (GC- 
FID Shimadzu GC-2010). Sulfuric acid and ethanol were used 
to acidify the samples and standards. A mixing ratio of 5:2:2 
(sample:ethanol:sulfuric acid) was used, followed by a 30-min 
incubation at 70 ◦C. The GC test was set up at a temper atur e of 
250 ◦C and a pr essur e of 62 kPa. The gas flow rate was 25 ml/min in 
total, with 3 ml/min for the purge flow. Additionally, the sampling 
rate was 40 ms, with a sample incubation temperature of 40 ◦C 
and a read time of 6 min. 
Enzyme activities 
Extr acellular enzyme pr oduction for bacterial isolates and for 
food waste before and after pr etr eatment was quantified via pub- 
lished methods . T he supernatant (filter ed thr ough a 0.22 μm filter) 
of pr etr eated food w aste w as used for the analysis. Samples for 
extracellular enzyme production at different growth stages were 
collected from isolates cultured for 1, 8 and 24 h at 30 ◦C with shak- 
ing at 160 rpm in LB10 medium. Arthrobacter koreensis and Bacillus 
stercoris were selected for an alternative collection schedule be- 
cause of their unique growth patterns. For these two strains, su- 
pernatant samples were collected at 3 h (instead of 8 h) for the lag 
phase. 
The enzyme quantification protocol can be summarized as fol- 
lows: the protease quantification method follo w ed the protocol 
of Sigma–Aldrich and used casein as the substrate (Cupp-Eny ar d 
2008 ). The cellulase activity was measured with carboxymethyl- 
cellulose in 0.05 M citrate buffer, and the absorbance was mea- 
sured at 540 nm (Jasani et al. 2016 ). Dinitrosalicylic acid was used 
as the colouring agent. Amylase activity quantification was per- 
formed according to a published method (Oliv eir a et al. 2019 ). 
Like cellulase, dinitrosalicylic acid was used, and the absorbance 
was measured at 540 nm. The lipase activity quantification as- 
say was performed according to a published protocol (Pinsirodom 
and Parkin 2001 ). Enzyme activities are measured as unit activ- 
ity per ml of supernatant. All chemicals w ere pur chased from 
Sigma −Aldrich unless specifically stated. 
DN A isola tion, sequencing, and quantitati v e PCR 
DN A isolation w as performed via the DNeasy Po w erSoil Kit (Qi- 
agen). The bacterial genetic copy abundance was quantified via 
qPCR (r eal-time pol ymer ase c hain r eaction) via the primers 1048F 
and 1194R. The thermal cycling settings were as follows: 3 min 
of denaturation at 98 ◦C, follo w ed b y 40 c ycles of DN A segment 
replication at 90 ◦C for 20 s and at 62 ◦C for 50 s . T he temper atur e 
was then decreased to 60 ◦C and maintained for 10 s for fluores- 
cent reads, follo w ed b y a temper atur e incr ease fr om 60 to 90 ◦C in 
0.5 ◦C intervals for melt curve analysis. 
Sequencing of the DN A w as carried out by the Ramaciotti Cen- 
ter (UNSW) on the 16S rRNA gene V4 region via the primer set 
515F&806R on the MiSeq V2 2 × 250 bp platform. P air ed-end se- 
quencing results were analysed via the QIIME II 2019.7 pipeline 
(Bolyen et al. 2019 ), and the sampling depth was set to 1600. The 
D ada 2 plugin (Callahan et al. 2016 ) was used to denoise the data, 
with the trimming length determined via FastQC for quality as- 
surance . T he sequencing results have been submitted to the NCBI 
Sequence Read Arc hiv e (accession number PRJNA805020). 
Biological methane potential assay 
The Automatic Methane Potential Test System (AMPTS II from 
Biopr ocess Contr ol) runs 15 samples in par allel. Eac h bottle con- 
tained 150 ml of digestate and 150 ml of either food waste slurry 
or water as blank contr ol. Fiv e gr oups eac h containing biological 
triplicates include water , prior -to-tr eatment food waste, untr eated 
food waste, aerated food waste, and aerated and pH-adjusted food 
waste . T he water sample consisted of 150 ml of digestate and 
150 ml of water. Prior to treatment, the food waste group was sup- 
plemented with 150 ml of food waste slurry with a solid content of 
5% and 150 ml of digestate prior to treatment. The treated groups

Results 
Highly abundant bacteria in food waste display 
limited extracellular enzyme production 
To assess the extracellular enzyme production of bacteria indige- 
nous to food waste, 17 bacterial strains isolated from food waste 
were tested for their extracellular enzyme activities via culture 
supernatants from different growth stages. Table 1 shows that 
24%–35% of the food waste isolates produced protease , amylase , 
and lipase activities exclusiv el y during the late gr owth sta ge and 
early stationary phase. Cellulase activity was observed in 88% of 
the isolates whose production was observed throughout different 
gr owth sta ges. Isolates r epr esenting some of the most abundant 
bacteria in food waste samples (Lactobacillaceae species Lactiplan- 
tibacillus plantarum and Leuconostoc mesenteriodes ) were only capa- 
ble of producing protease and cellulase at relatively low amounts 
during the stationary phase, suggesting that the bacterial commu- 
nity indigenous to food waste has low potential for extracellular 
enzyme production. 
Food waste pretreatment impacts volatile fatty 
acid production and bacterial abundance 
To examine the impacts of pH neutralization and aeration on the 
indigenous microbial community of food waste, samples were in- 
cubated for 3 days with pH adjustment alone, aeration alone, or 
a combination of both. Table 2 shows that pH adjustment, aer- 
ation alone, or in combination resulted in significantly higher 
pr opionate concentr ations (av er a ging 69.0, 65.3, and 103.3 mM 
compared with 14.0 mM in the untreated group and 21.0 mM 
in the prior-to-treatment group) and that pH adjustment with 
or without aeration resulted in significantly higher butyrate con- 
centr ations (av er a ging 106.7, 12.0, and 41.5 mM compar ed with 
0 mM in both untreated and prior-to-treatment groups). Accom-

Pretreatment increased Proteobacteria and 
decreased Lactobacillaceae abundance 
The impact of pr etr eatment on the micr obial comm unity compo- 
sition after 3 days was examined by sequencing 16S rRNA genes 
in DNA extracts from food waste samples . T he composition of 
the untreated samples was similar to that of food waste prior to 
pr etr eatment (Fig. 2 and Supplementary Fig. 1 ). pH adjustment, 
aeration, or a combination of both resulted in shifts in commu- 
nity composition on the basis of principal coordinate analysis 
( Supplementary Fig. 2 ). All the treatments significantly increased 
the proportion of Proteobacteria (Fig. 2 ). pH adjustment increased 
the r elativ e abundance of Pr oteobacteria fr om 0.3% ± 0.1% in un- 
treated samples to 44% ± 15% ( P = 0.02). Aeration increased the 
r elativ e abundance of Proteobacteria from 0.3% ± 0.1% in the un- 
treated samples to 28.0% ± 23.0% ( P = 0.08). The combined treat- 
ment increased the relative abundance of Proteobacteria from 
0.3% ± 0.1% in the untreated samples to 57.0% ± 16.0% ( P = 0.01). 
The increase in Proteobacteria was driven by the increase in 
Gamma pr oteobacteria, including an unclassified lineage within 
the Enter obacteriaceae famil y and Pseudomonas psyc hrophile in the 
Pseudomonadaceae famil y. A positiv e corr elation ( R 2 = 0.92) was 
observed between the relative abundance of Enterobacteriaceae 
and the pr opionate concentr ation ( Supplementary Fig. 3 ). The rel- 
ative abundances of Lactobacillaceae , Leuconostocaceae , and Lis- 
teriaceae decreased during pretreatment. pH was negatively cor- 
related ( R 2 = 0.78) with the relative abundance of Lactobacillaceae 
( Supplementary Fig. 3 ). 
Pretreated food waste is more susceptible to 
anaerobic digestion 
Biological methane potential tests were used to assess the im- 
pact of pr etr eatment on food waste anaerobic digestion (Fig. 3 ). 
Methane pr oduction fr om food waste prior to pr etr eatment was 
biphasic, with r a pid methane pr oduction occurring ov er 5 days 
follo w ed b y a slo w r ate of methane pr oduction ov er the ensuing 
20 da ys . Food waste pr etr eated for 3 days with aer ation pr oduced 
the most methane (av er a ging 1000 ml), and methane production 
was complete within 20 da ys . pH adjustment of aerated samples 
did not provide additional benefits to methane generation. The 
methane pr oduction pr ofile of food waste samples that were in- 
cubated for 3 days without aeration or pH adjustment (untreated) 
was similar to that of food waste samples prior to pr etr eatment 
(r elativ el y slow and ongoing after 25 days at r oughl y 750 ml). 
Discussion 
The de v elopment of pr etr eatment methods to enhance the anaer- 
obic digestion of organic feedstocks such as food waste is a long- 
standing r esearc h endeavour. Tr aditionall y, methods that harness 
the enzymatic activities of micr oor ganisms indigenous to food 
waste, suc h as aer ation, hav e been de v eloped via a top-down ap- 
pr oac h, paying little attention to the composition of microbial 
communities and the relevant characteristics of specific microbial 
linea ges. When micr obiology has been inv estigated, a tr aditional 
cultiv ation-based a ppr oac h has been taken, which is limited by 
widel y r ecognized cultiv ation biases (Hassa et al. 2018 ). 
We have taken a bottom-up a ppr oac h to enhancing food waste 
digestion, viewing food waste and its micr oflor a as an ecosystem, 
wher e emer gent functions ar e dependent on micr obial comm u- 
nity composition. In a pr e vious study, we c har acterized the indige- 
nous micr oflor a of food waste via contemporary DNA sequencing 
(Tang et al. 2023 ). This r e v ealed that food waste comm unities ar e 
dominated by bacteria within the Firmicutes phylum, which are 
known for the production of organic acids that stave off competi- 
tors b y lo w ering the pH (König and F r öhlic h 2017 ). Mor eov er, bac- 
teria within the phylum Pr oteobacteria, whic h is known for its role 
in food spoila ge thr ough extr acellular enzyme pr oduction, wer e 
noticeabl y absent. Corr elations between high Firmicutes abun- 
dance and low abundance of Pr oteobacteria hav e pr e viousl y been 
observed in the beginning of anaerobic digestion (Wu et al. 2016 ). 
We ther efor e hypothesized that common pr etr eatments for en- 
hanced anaerobic digestion, such as aeration and pH adjustment, 
ar e effectiv e because the y enhance the competiti v e fitness of Pr o- 
teobacteria over Firmicutes in food waste ecosystems.

Enterobacteriaceae and Pseudomonadaceae families increased 
in r elativ e abundance, wher eas linea ges within the Leuconos-

Aer ation r esulted in an increase in pH and bacterial abundance, 
wher eas pH neutr alization alone or with aeration did not increase 
bacterial abundance . T he shift to w ar ds incr eased r elativ e abun- 
dance of Proteobacteria is ther efor e consider ed to be a function 
of pH, but the pH c hange driv en by aeration is more conducive 
to growth within the 3-day incubation period. This finding can 
motiv ate the de v elopment of methods to incr ease pr oteobacterial 
abundance. 
Aeration and pH neutralization affected the VFA profile of the 
food waste samples. Initially, formate followed by propionate was 
the most abundant VFA. Aeration and pH neutralization resulted 
in a decrease in formate concentration and an increase in propi- 
onate concentr ation. Pr oteobacteria may be associated with for- 
mate consumption and pr opionate pr oduction. According to v ari- 
ous studies on VFA production, a pH of 5–6 favours propionic acid 
pr oduction, wher eas a pH < 5 or > 6 favours butyric acid pro- 
duction (Sun et al. 2021 ). In both the aerated and/or pH-adjusted 
groups, the butyric acid concentration was greater than that in 
the aerated and untreated groups. High propionic acid produc- 
tion could also be linked to increased abundances of Clostridia, 
Beta pr oteobacteria, and Bacter oidetes (Zhou et al. 2020b ). 
Ho w e v er, within a complicated environment such as food 
waste, the concentration of VFAs will not be solely defined by pro- 
duction but will also be impacted by microbial consumption. For- 
mate mainly comes from sugar fermentation by Enter obacter ales 
(Leonhartsber ger et al. 2002 ), wher eas acetate can be fermented 
fr om pr opionate and butyr ate (Zhang et al. 2009 ). Anaer obicall y, 
acetate can be used as a building block for butyrate (Duncan et al. 
2004 ). Propionate can also be generated under aerobic conditions 
during food spoilage (Nychas et al. 2008 ). Acetate can be oxidized 
into longer carbon chain VFAs (Zhou et al. 2018 ). Longer carbon 
c hain VFAs, suc h as butyr ate, can be tr ansformed into pr opionate 
and acetate and vice versa (Duncan et al. 2004 ). This could ex- 
plain the observation that a decrease in butyrate accompanied 
an increase in propionate when the pH was adjusted and when 
the pH was adjusted and aerated. Formic acid can be used as an 
energy source for biological activities and is thus depleted after 
3 days regardless of tr eatment. Gamma pr oteobacteria can me- 
tabolize formate (Zhou et al. 2020b ), and propionate production 
is possible with an ele v ated abundance of Clostridium (Isipato et 
al. 2020 ). The lack of acetic acid could be the result of bacterial 
metabolism that ultimately hinders the dominance of lactic acid 
bacteria, whic h pr oduce lar ge amounts of acetic acid (Peinemann 
et al. 2020 ). Longer carbon chain VFAs may be derived from larger 
fatty acids being broken down into smaller VFAs during acidogen- 
esis (Zhang et al. 2005 , Liang et al. 2024 ). With more complex food 
waste substrates being transformed into various VFAs, pretreated 
food waste is more digestible during the anaerobic digestion pro- 
cess and has greater stability (Xu et al. 2021 ). 
Enzymes produced by bacteria are essential for food waste di- 
gestion. Compared with the untreated samples, pretreated food 
waste resulted in greater digestive enzyme activity in biological 
methane potential tests over 25 days. The common hydraulic re- 
tention time for anaerobic food waste digestion is between 20 and 
30 days (Zhang and Jahng 2012 ). The fact that methane production 
fr om pr etr eated food waste plateaus in < 20 days with increased 
methane pr oduction compar ed with untr eated food waste v al- 
idates the effectiveness of pr etr eatment (Montalvo et al. 2016 , 
Cheng et al. 2021 ). 
In summary, this study r e v ealed that aer ation or pH neutr al- 
ization pr etr eatment of food waste for 3 days resulted in a strong 
shift in the micr obial comm unity to w ar ds Proteobacteria. This 
was associated with increased extracellular enzyme activity and 
mor e efficient anaer obic digestion (r educed r etention time). These 
findings suggest that manipulation of environmental parameters 
in food waste to promote the growth of Proteobacteria or artificial 
ele v ation of proteobacterial abundance through bioaugmentation 
can generate superior anaerobic digestion results.
